analysis.one_liner: Protects the Arctic refuge coastal plain as wilderness and repeals its oil drilling program.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 140 House cosponsors, died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cancel the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge oil and gas program created by the 2017 tax law, which set up drilling lease sales on the refuge's coastal plain. It would also permanently designate about 1.56 million acres of that plain as federal wilderness, barring all development there. The House never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who value protected public lands, wildlife habitat, and keeping one of the nation's largest wild areas unspoiled. The Gwich'in people, whose way of life is tied to the caribou herd that calves on the coastal plain, have long supported wilderness protection there, though that is not stated in the bill text itself.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People who value protected public lands

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the oil and gas program for the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge that the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act created, ending the mandated lease sales on the refuge's coastal plain.

Designates approximately 1,559,538 acres of the refuge's coastal plain in Alaska as wilderness under the Wilderness Act, which permanently bars roads, motorized equipment, and commercial development in the area.

Once land is designated wilderness, the protection cannot be undone by a future administration's policy change — only by another act of Congress — so the refuge's fate would no longer hinge on who holds the White House.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies that wanted to drill the coastal plain, and the federal and Alaska treasuries, which would forgo royalties and revenue from lease sales that the 2017 law was designed to generate.

drawbacks.text: Repealing Section 20001 of the 2017 tax law would cancel lease sales that were projected to bring the federal government revenue and royalties, some of which flow to Alaska — a real fiscal cost, though small relative to the federal budget.

Wilderness designation is effectively permanent: it would foreclose drilling on about 1.56 million acres no matter what future energy conditions look like, which critics called locking out resources before the full oil potential was known.
Some Alaska communities supported the drilling program for the jobs, revenue, and local benefits it promised; the bill offers them no replacement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The conservation gain is large and permanent: protecting one of the last untouched Arctic ecosystems, with global wildlife value, at a modest one-time fiscal cost. The forgone drilling revenue is real but small in national terms. The honest trade-off is that wilderness designation is irreversible, so the decision forecloses energy development there forever even if circumstances change.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Natural Resources Committee and its subcommittees for the entire two-year Congress and was never brought up for a vote.

narrative.text: Representative Jared Huffman introduced the bill on February 4, 2021, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
It drew 140 cosponsors — 139 Democrats and one Republican, Representative Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania.
On March 1, 2021, the bill was referred to two subcommittees, Energy and Mineral Resources and National Parks, Forests, and Public Lands.
No markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred; the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
The Senate never considered the bill; the House is where it stalled.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies and officials who wanted to drill the refuge's coastal plain are better off, because the 2017 drilling program the bill would have repealed remains on the books and the wilderness designation never happened.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Backers of Arctic coastal plain drilling

for.name: Rep. Jared Huffman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the refuge oil and gas program and designate the coastal plain as wilderness.

for.name: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick
for.what_they_did: Was the bill's sole Republican cosponsor among the original 50 members listed at introduction.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and, along with its Energy and Mineral Resources and National Parks subcommittees, never reported it out or scheduled any vote during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic: 139 of the 140 cosponsors were Democrats, with only Rep. Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania crossing party lines.

industries.note: The bill would repeal the drilling program created by the 2017 tax law and permanently bar development on the coastal plain, ending the industry's access to a large prospective oil region. The industry's gain from drilling — royalties, leases, and production — is exactly what the bill's protection would take away, so its interest runs against the public's interest in preserving the refuge.
